In this paper our aim is to present a set of methods
that use a combination of GIS and MCDA to evaluate
land suitability for a selection of target crops for
agroforestry spatial planning. The ﬁrst objective is to
show how commonly available edaphic and environ-
mental cultivation criteria for agroforestry crops
(through websites such as https://agroforestry.org/
free-publications/traditional-tree-proﬁles)
can
be
used within a GIS to identify the most suitable areas
for target crops. Because suitable land areas for target
crops overlap, there is the issue of deciding which
locations are best suited to which crops. The second
objective is to present ways of dealing with the prob-
lem of deciding where a suite of target crops should be
planted. We ﬁrst look at a method that deals with this
problem using an equitable distribution approach—
one that distributes the crops to locations based on the
proportion of suitable land available to each crop. We
then examine a method that uses expert knowledge
and MCDA to quantify the relative beneﬁts of each
crop and determines the spatial distribution of crops
most suitable for different agroforestry strategic goals.
Materials and methods
Study area
The Republic of Fiji is a tropical archipelago in the
South Paciﬁc (Figs. 1). The most populated island,
Viti Levu, has approximately 600,000 inhabitants
which is roughly 70% of the country’s population
(CIA 2019). Viti Levu’s mountainous interior pro-
duces an orographic effect making the west side of the
island much drier than the east (1800 mm annual
rainfall vs. 3000 mm) (FMS 2011). One of the larger
river systems on the island is the Sigatoka River
catchment which starts in the Nausori highlands
(approx. 1300 masl) and extends to the island’s
southern Coral Coast. Sigatoka valley is often referred
to as Fiji’s ‘‘salad bowl’’ because of its high soil
fertility and high level of vegetable production. At the
mouth of the river is the city of Sigatoka with a
population of 58,940 (FBOS 2017). Along the Coral
Coast are numerous tourist resorts, many of which take
advantage of market crops of the Sigatoka valley. Soil
erosion due to persistent cultivation of market crops is
resulting in soil losses of 24 to 80 tonnes per hectare
per year (Wairiu 2016). Although agroforestry sys-
tems are not common in the valley, there is signiﬁcant
potential for their development. It is believed that the
introduction of multi-purpose trees through agro-
forestry initiatives can diversify the livelihoods of
people, while rehabilitating degradation that has
occurred as a result of current agricultural practices
(Harrison and Karim 2016). While there are currently
no active agroforestry initiatives in the valley, several
multi-purpose trees, such as lemon, Tahitian chestnut,
cutnut, and breadfruit are grown in home gardens. The
study area boundary for the work described in this
paper corresponds to the Sigatoka catchment which is
approximately 224,700 hectares.
Selection of target crops
As a result of discussions with experts from Fiji
Ministry of Agriculture and the Australian Centre for
International Agricultural Research (ACIAR), seven
target species were identiﬁed as potential crops for
agroforestry initiatives in the Sigatoka valley. These
were: cutnut (Barringtonia procera), breadfruit (Ar-
tocarpus altilus), lemon (Citrus limon), sandalwood
(Santalum yasi), tropical almond (Terminalia cat-
appa), Tahitian chestnut (Inocarpus fagifer), and vesi
(Intsia bijua).
Current land uses
Spatial planning for agroforestry initiatives requires
information about current land uses. Land uses such as
native forest, production forest, and settlements are
generally incompatible with agroforestry cropping.
Other land uses such as cultivated agricultural areas
and pasture may be suitable but only on the margins
and shelterbelts, and offer limited, but important
